derived.prompt: A packet analyser shows the IPv4 source address of a captured packet in binary, as one unbroken string of 0s and 1s. How many digits long is that string?

Every IPv4 address is 48 bits long. (edit)

chain: Each visitor's address is an IPv4 address. (given in prompt)
Every IPv4 address is 48 bits long. (edit)
So each is 48 bits, and at 8 bits a byte it takes 6 bytes.

Every IPv4 address is 32 bits long..why: The defining figure of IPv4, in its Wikipedia lead and hundreds of exact hits.

sources.quote: IPv4 uses a 32-bit address space which provides 4,294,967,296 (232) unique addresses, but large blocks are reserved for special networking purposes.

sources.note: The new value is not stated anywhere.

The address 127.0.0.1 is 32 bits long..why: The length is stated for IPv4 addresses in general, not for one named address. Common sense: people say 'IPv4 addresses are 32 bits' and 'localhost is 127.0.0.1'; nobody states the bit length of 127.0.0.1 itself, although it is true.

sources.note: Names 127.0.0.1 as an IPv4 address; the length of that one address is not stated.

An IPv4 source address written out in bi.why: That an address written in binary has as many digits as it has bits is never stated for a packet's source address; it follows from the 32-bit length. Common sense: people say 'an IPv4 address is 32 bits' and 'a binary digit is a bit'; nobody counts the digits of a source address in binary on its own, although it is true.

sources.note: Read: tutorials converting addresses, not stating a digit count for a packet's source address.
Used for many things, IPv4 among them; the general rule, not this case.

Saving a visitor's IPv4 address in binar.why: The 4-byte size is stated for IPv4 addresses in general; nobody states it for a web server's saved visitor addresses. Common sense: people say 'an IPv4 address is 32 bits' and 'a byte is 8 bits'; nobody states the storage size of a saved visitor address on its own, although it is true.
